description: We are growing software engineering students who enjoy turning real data into something people can use. Our project, Earth Jukebox, turns NASA Earth data into music and is built with React, TypeScript and Tone.js, with accessibility as a core goal. Join us if you like web development, audio, data visualisation, accessibility testing or clear storytelling. We are especially looking for a blind or low-vision tester and anyone who can help with design and demo polish.
summary:
What we developed: 
Earth Jukebox is a web app that turns real NASA Earth data into music, in the browser and in real time. It reads NASA GIBS sea surface temperature maps pixel by pixel, converts each colour to an estimated temperature using NASA’s own colour table, and plays the map west to east like a score: warm ocean sounds higher and brighter, cold ocean lower and darker, and land is silent. The same engine also plays monthly vegetation data and 45 years of NASA POWER temperature for any coordinates, one note per year.

How it addresses the challenge: 
It pairs NASA Earth visual frames with live sonification, as the challenge asks, and treats accessibility as a core goal. Every sound comes with plain text, a chart and a data table, and the app works by keyboard and screen reader, with no autoplay. A separate NASA POWER dataset checks that the music follows real seasons.

Why it matters:
 Maps exclude blind and low-vision people and hide change over time. Earth Jukebox gives the same science a second form, and states its limits honestly, including when a local trend is weak.
details:
What does your project do, and how does it work?
Earth Jukebox turns real NASA Earth data into music, live in the browser. Pick a year and the app loads 12 monthly NASA GIBS sea surface temperature frames and measures their colours on a hidden canvas. Each colour is converted to an estimated temperature using NASA’s own colour table. The map is then read west to east like a score: warmer ocean gives higher, brighter notes in a major mood, colder ocean gives lower, darker notes in a minor mood, and land and ice are silent. The same engine also plays monthly vegetation (NDVI) and, in “Hear your place”, 45 years of NASA POWER temperature for any coordinates, one note per year, with the local trend stated in plain words.

What benefits does it have?
NASA’s maps are visual, so blind and low-vision users, and anyone who can’t tell similar colours apart, are left out. Every sound here has a text description, a chart and a data table beside it, so nobody has to use sound to get the science. It works by keyboard and screen reader, never plays audio by itself, and includes a playable map explorer and a listening test.

What is the intended impact?
To make Earth science reach more people, and to make its claims checkable. A separate NASA POWER dataset checks that the music follows real seasonal temperatures. The app reports honest results, including a place where the local trend is weak, instead of forcing a warming story.

What tools did you use?
TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Tone.js (sound) and Recharts (charts), deployed on Vercel. Everything runs in the browser, with no server or accounts. Data: NASA GIBS, NASA Worldview and NASA POWER. AI assistance (Claude) helped with code, tests, slides and documentation, as stated in our README.

How is your project creative?
A map becomes a musical score. Strips of longitude become melody steps, the southern ocean becomes the bass, and sharp temperature changes become small grace notes. All notes use one pentatonic scale, so the result is pleasant, and the same frame always gives the same music, so comparisons are fair.

What factors did your team consider?
Accessibility, musical quality, honesty about limits, and reliability. Colours are estimates, each frame is a daily snapshot, and the music is a creative translation, not the real sound of the ocean. Failed frames are retried, and a missing month is labelled instead of breaking the year. We have not yet tested with blind or low-vision users, and we say so in the README.
